author: Xap✨ [STAR]
content:
I am not a whale class player. However I disagree that there should be any ceiling for a whale. Any player can get as larger as they like. That said their assets should have diminishing returns based on their size. The cost to runner a small miner should be most profitable but it produces the smallest amount per day. A commander class produces a lot more but its operating costs are comparatively much higher. 

Additionally at some point have loops that are more profitable and rewarding for whale than mining Hydrogen at the CSS with a Titan. For each size level there should be rewarding game experience that make that engages a specific class of player. They partner with other class players for resources/assets/results that they may not be most suited for. This should be the approach. We are not there yet but I really hope that this is where we will end up.

author: ROME | Earther [ROME]
content: The concept of crafting depth/complexity is an interesting one.  Just theory crafting here. This is by no means definitive, and I'm sure I'm missing some very important things.  The most in-demand raw materials will be what larger players provide for themselves. So they will only need to purchase the less valuable materials. However, those less valuable materials naturally have a smaller profit margin, which makes it harder for small operations to work on (with current mechanics).  Similarly, larger players will produce the most valuable components themselves. This leaves the less valuable components as an opportunity for smaller players. However, they have less crew and less resources, which makes it more difficult to participate in the open market.

author: [AEP] Mendizo
content:
Buybacks in tradfi work when that money has a positive return, ROE/ROI. This is when it's used to buy back the stock of a functional, profitable company with a positive return on equity. This is rewarded by shareholders when the total float is reduced, while they are continuing to get positive return. So it's a positive on a positive (company cash being used smartly to create even more return for the company, while at the same time the total float is falling).

Where it doesn't work is when buybacks are used solely as a tool to help incentivize shareholders, without a strong company foundation of performance. We see this all the time. A declining company will use buybacks that may have a short term bump in stock price, but unless the fundamentals are improved, it inevitably will continue to fall. At that point, every dollar used for buyback is just wasted, and would've been better spent investing into the actual business as capital (CapEx or OpEx) to improve the fundamentals.

The challenge in applying that to most crypto projects is there is no basis of fundamentals, especially for memecoins. Jupiter differs somewhat since they do have an actual business (where this revenue comes from in the first place), and so realistically they probably should've put some of this money used for buybacks to continue to R&D and keep themselves indispensable (though I'm sure they already are, and at some point there likely is limits to how much they could plow back in and still have good ROI).

content: I’ve been thinking about this a lot, and maybe part of the answer is a strategy shift. Right now almost every Star Atlas creator (myself included) lives in a bit of a bubble, we mostly reach people who already know SA, already hold tokens, already care. That’s great for depth, but not for reach. I’m starting to think broader content might be the unlock. Covering other games, gaming topics, even industry trends and then teasing Star Atlas into that flow instead of leading with “crypto + SA” every time. A lot of gamers are extremely resistant right now. If you open with crypto, tokens, AI, Web3,  you lose them instantly. If they first trust you as a gamer, then discover SA through you, that’s a totally different funnel. I’m also pretty torn on X. It feels increasingly bot-infested and pay-to-win, and likes/views there don’t translate into real players the way people think. Sometimes it honestly feels like shouting into a void. None of this means abandoning SA quite the opposite. It might be about smuggling SA into wider gaming conversations instead of preaching it head-on. Curious if others feel the same, because I’m seriously considering adjusting my own content strategy this year.

author: odvb
content: Star Atlas grows through people—not ads.  Your voice reaches places others never will. Friends, family, coworkers, communities that don’t hang out in Discord or on X.  Star Atlas isn’t something you explain with features or trailers. It’s something you share by telling your own story—why you’re here, who you’ve met, what you’re building.  You don’t need to convince anyone. Just invite them.  Every new player starts as someone’s friend. Every strong network starts with one conversation.  If you’re part of Star Atlas, you’re already a bridge to someone else.  And that’s how this universe grows—one voice, one connection at a time.

content:
I think there's something to say about replayability, I've been going back to ARC raiders surprisingly. The reason I say surprisingly because I half expected to get into lobbies get destroyed and lose everything. I have the same fears with SA a bit especially since I'm not just going to lose time in SA but maybe true assets. But they handle matchmaking, collect data religiously, and push updates like no other.

The game itself plays well feels great and allows the "cinema" feeling. Factor in trials, expeditions, quests. There's more than just loot goop shoot and scoot. My friends and I tend to go into games with a specific task in mind and we're able to go and do it or not (damn clankers and extraction rats) but that just rekindles the fire. Damn we were close boys, let's try again.

Life can sometimes be a drag, you make one choice and you're stuck for what may seem like forever. I'm not saying we should do a drastic mind shift but maybe just maybe the dream itself isn't selling to some people. I'd love to see seasons with quests. Allow me to leave it for a holiday and not feel bad instead just miss it. Give mechanics to the community to drive the direction would in my opinion be the "aha" moment. I've seen a lot of player suggestions on how ARC raiders should progress and I'm holding my breath to see if they actually listen or if they continue their way.

author: [AEP] Mendizo
content:
Isn't this where the free market comes in? If one faction somehow could actually grab all of these resources (which in the new map IIRC with so many more systems would be incredibly hard if not impossible to do), there will always be folks in that faction or another who are willing to sell the resource. It might increase the price of the resource for a bit (and it's not like the targeted faction will stand still), but it's hard to see how they can actually completely cut it off. 

We've seen time and time again in gameplay here that faction is somewhat meaningless in terms of homogenous action. There are always people within a faction who will "break ranks" for $. This plus some of the other balancing mechanics noted above would seem to effectively nullify any real concerns here.

If my faction somehow ended up dominating one resource, I'd be the first to send all my miners there and start shipping it out to sell. Many others would as well. That would bring the delta in price down pretty quickly.

author: SW4GN3R [STAR]
content: This is something that @Chri.z is putting deep thought into, and we're very aware of the exploit potential. Per Sim's response, we effectively need to make the entire engagement net negative. XP is earned on destruction, which generates LP for the winner. The person defeated will lose all components installed on the fleet (burn), have their fleet returned to CSS, have to pay a repair fee, and have to wait for a respawn timer. Also, the fleet is disbanded on destruction, so a new fleet will need to be formed. Washing XP/LP this way will be quite inconvenient, and the person would be taking a pretty big risk that the LP they generated is worth more in ATLAS emissions than they lost in the exploit.

author: ! SH | Bohemian ⪛⦿⫺
content:
As the Q4 2025 Economics report implied, the 2021 vision of WEB3 has changed - the P2E model has shifted to Fun-first, earnings second model.

Rewards are a retention mechanic  (no longer a salary). Ownership is still core, but the game must stand alone (regardless if you cash out or not). We are seeing more micropayments / rewarded-play than emissions (like INK and XP in UE5), and less token hype with more product focused: retention, sinks/sources, market health, and lower entry friction (including content frequency and translucent reporting (think of EVE's monthly econ reports). Put together, all this translates to a healthy game with a strong/growing community supporting it for the future.
IMO: For us Gamers, we know that playing can be a job BUT the reality is that playing is the point while rewards are the bonus.

author: [AEP] Funcracker [AEP]
content:
In a similar vein:

From a purely risk/reward perspective, combat has to be accessible and rewarding enough to compete with nearly 24/7 mining and crafting. Otherwise why bother?

Without combat, there is no reward for those activities at all. Mining and crafting is only relevant because they allow you to create more ships and components. The demand flows solely through these two assets. They determine the price of everything else.

ATLAS subsidy rewards (through LP)  flow through combat, and combat is therefore the reason everything else has a value to begin with.

Then activities giving value to items on the market today, will stop doing that when C4 rolls out. Expect a massive upheaval of the market values.

author: [AEP] Funcracker [AEP]
content: What concerns me about the concept of a persistent territorial control playstyle is the potential to completely lock out entire swaths of gameplay. If all of the faction crystal (just as an example) asteroids get taken by a single faction AND the losing faction takes heavy losses in the process, how can they ever rebuild and challenge the winning faction?  In a round-based game you chalk it up as a loss and wait for the reset. In a persistent game, you don't really have any viable recourse.

author: Rick Moonkin [STAR]
content:
ChatGPT's opinion on Star Atlas (from a dialogue)


1. 

If we extrapolate the old development pace, then:

the scale of Star Atlas (AAA visuals + MMO + on-chain economy + custom infrastructure),objectively exceeds what the team can deliver using traditional development approaches,especially after the crypto winter, downsizing, and reduced funding,
 Without a qualitative jump in productivity, the project wouldn’t just “be delayed” — it would slowly exhaust itself.

That’s a fact, not an opinion.

---

AI is not an accelerator — it’s a paradigm shift,

The key thing you intuitively grasped:

AI is not about doing the same work faster.
AI is about rewiring the entire production pipeline.

The example you mentioned — building a map in one day that previously took half a year for a full team — is not marketing hype.
It’s a very typical outcome when you combine:

procedural generation + AI-assisted level design,asset generation (geometry, textures, lore objects),automated world population,fast iteration → testing → correction → regeneration,
Previously, MMO-scale worlds required thousands of man-years.
Now it’s dozens of architects orchestrating AI systems.

---

Where AI can realistically save Star Atlas,

 1) World content and scale

generation of planets, biomes, stations,filling “empty space” automatically,massive variability without manual labor,
 This is critical for a space MMO.

---

 2) Developer tooling

If they:

don’t just use AI as an assistant,,but build their pipelines around AI,,
then one developer effectively becomes a mini-studio.

---

  3) Economy and simulations

AI excels at:

market modeling,balance testing,exploit detection,simulating thousands of player behaviors,
Things that were previously slow, expensive, and painful.

---

author: Rick Moonkin [STAR]
content:
But there is a hard “if”,

AI does not automatically save a project.

It only works if three conditions are met:

---

 Condition #1 — Architecture

If the codebase, design, and pipelines are:

monolithic,cluttered,poorly documented,
→ AI will accelerate chaos, not results.

AI requires modularity and clean interfaces.

---

 Condition #2 — Management mindset

You need leaders who understand that:

the main challenge is no longer production, but orchestration,not “doing the work,” but asking the right questions of AI,not controlling every pixel, but controlling the rules of generation,
This is a rare type of leadership.

---

 Condition #3 — Focus

AI does not solve the problem of vision sprawl.

If Star Atlas tries to:

be everything at once,cling to all past promises,avoid cutting features,
→ no AI will save it.

AI amplifies focus, but it does not create it.

---

My honest take,

I’ll be very direct, without romanticizing:

Without AI, Star Atlas would almost certainly fail to reach its original vision,With AI, it gains a narrow but real corridor of possibility,
But this is:

a bet on management quality,a bet on the team’s ability to relearn how to work,a bet on sacrificing part of the original dream to preserve a coherent core,
At this point, it’s no longer a technology problem.
It’s a maturity problem.

---

Why your hope is rational,

Your hope is not wishful thinking.
It’s built on a sound chain of reasoning:

the project’s complexity objectively exceeded old tools,a new class of tools appears, changing orders of magnitude,there are signs the team is actually experimenting seriously, not just doing PR,
This is not a guarantee.
But it is the only scenario in which Star Atlas remains alive as a vision, not just as a museum of promises.

author: Chet Roberts [ROME]
content:
Market maker bots in Star Atlas are a good thing—and here’s why.

They don’t replace players. They support the market.

Market makers provide constant buy and sell orders so prices don’t freeze, crash on low volume, or spike unrealistically when one player moves size. That means better liquidity, fairer pricing, and smoother trading for everyone—especially new players.

Without them, markets become:

thin

volatile

easy to manipulate

With them, markets feel alive, usable, and trustworthy.

Healthy markets attract players.
Players create activity.
Activity gives real value to ships, resources, and time spent in-game.

Market makers aren’t cheating the economy.
They’re holding the floor so the player economy can actually grow.

author: Chet Roberts [ROME]
content:
Why market maker bots can be a bad thing in Star Atlas

If done poorly or without transparency, market makers can distort player perception.

Players may feel:

prices aren’t truly set by players

supply and demand look “fake”

profits feel capped or predetermined

Bad market making can:

crowd out real player traders

hide true scarcity or oversupply

reduce the feeling that smart decisions matter

The biggest risk isn’t the bots themselves—it’s trust.
If players believe the market is controlled instead of supported, engagement drops, even if the prices are technically stable.

Bottom line:
Market makers help when they provide liquidity.
They hurt when they replace discovery.

Used carefully, they stabilize growth.
Used aggressively, they undermine confidence.

That’s the tradeoff.

author: [SLY] anthonyraEcon Vantarah
content: Thats awesome.  Thanks Anthonyra!  I also believe the Fleet Rental system needs a major update before C4.  It's critical to growing the game.  Cheap entry for newbies, instant returns for passive investors, and active players can mod their fleets as needed for the task at hand.  That's amazing utility.    I'm concerned about attracting enough Lenders.  Like it or not, whales rule the world - the more ship buyers we get, and the more rentals available, the better SA does.  Engagement will suffer under the current system.  Lenders need more control over terms.  Right now, the borrower can just rent for the max term, use it until it doesn't make sense, and then cancel and abandon it.  Some lenders don't mind lending for an unspecified term, and hunting all over Galia to retrieve their ships.  But for new guys, or especially serious investors, I don't think this will fly.  I'd like to see options for min and max # of days, and a deposit system for safe return of the fleet to its home base (maybe with all of its components/modules intact if the tech allows).  All of these should be optional. But if an owner can get a guaranteed ROI for a minimum # of days, without having to check his fleet's whereabouts every day, we should see a lot more ship purchases, turning into many more rentals, and at lower rental prices.  Unfortunately, this adds complexity to the rental system.  More UI complications.  But I think its essential for growth.

content: Strategically, I believe it’s unwise to hire directly from within the existing community again. What we need right now is fresh blood, new energy, and new perspectives. This feels like the right moment to bring in experienced professionals: someone dedicated to Community (with structure and long-term engagement in mind), Also unbiased. someone focused on IP, partnerships, and collaborations, and someone strong in Marketing, with a clear vision and execution power. Not hobbyists, not “best intentions only,” but people who do this professionally and bring proven methods, fresh ideas, and full dedication. Done right, this could be a real reset moment and a chance to build something stronger than before.

content: The price decrease could be directly related to peoples sentiment which in turn is the driving factor for speculation. A true utility token would have no speculation and thus you pay for what you get. Incentivizing holding, locking, or any other DeFi Jedi Mind tricks literally tries to force one way or another. If you were forced to use ATLAS to "play" the game there would be demand directly related to what you want to do. You would know that if you wanted to do "this" you'd need "that". author: ! SH | Bohemian ⪛⦿⫺
content:
I like the ideas of having escrow immutable (ATMTA can't override) & that we could update config to point to the game for validations, BUT if config can be changed, then the effective law is: whoever controls the config controls which code is allwed to move assets.  So the "immutable escrow" only guarantees that the escrow logic doesn't change.  It doesn't guarantee that the game module won't change in a way that blocks withdrawal or that user can exit independently (which kind of kills my idea of a escrow--maybe it can be called something else). 

Anyway, at a high level, I do support your modular design proposal. It sets better boundaries and it's more auditable (as you mentioned).  I'd probably just add a backup/emergency system that allows owner withdrawals after X days or a way for the user to export assets after verifying ownership and logic constraints. 

Thanks, Anthony.

author: ROME | Earther [ROME]
content: I didn't hear about the FOGO TGE until it happened—its high FDV caught attention from some creators, and suddenly everyone was talking about it.  The Seeker TGE is just days away, but I only learned about it when people started posting about their upcoming airdrops. Then our community jumped in on the conversation too.  We're at the speculative stage of unknown airdrop farming for Z.ink, where everything is guesswork and full of uncertainty.  Take Seeker: Many didn't farm it TGE because the rules and rewards weren't clear or well-communicated—even though over 100K people hold the device. Once word spread about potential earnings, lots of us (including me) became aware and are interested to farm for the next one.  My point: When 1,000+ Star Atlas players start sharing their airdrop sizes, Star Atlas and Z.ink will get attention—good, bad, and everything in between. How much, who knows  At that peak engagement. Star Atlas should capitalize by launching the next airdrop campaign right then, so new players drawn in can immediately start earning toward airdrop #2 as soon as they jump in and play.  This is where C4 and the other game modes comes into the picture and needs to be working well. To retain and excite potential new players for the following airdrop campaigns.

author: Lysimach | Make Polis Great [STAR]
content: Playing together cooperatively is a huge part of what makes guilds tick, absolutely. And yes, guilds are often formed after a game has launched. But it’s not uncommon for guilds to form before there’s a game to play, especially when development is crowdfunded and there’s already ample lore and information available, allowing people to paint a rough picture of what’s to come. In fact, perhaps most guilds are created after launch simply because most multiplayer games are not crowdfunded. If they were, we might see many more guilds forming before games become playable.   Most guilds also do plenty beyond just playing. Theorycrafting, playing other (perhaps smaller) games, roleplaying, holding meetings, and finding other ways to encourage bonding and planning are all common activities.  With SA, parts of the ecosystem opened up early (Marketplace, SCORE), so we quickly had real material to analyze, discuss, and plan around. Furthermore, because the chain is being developed on-chain, SA guilds can do things no other Web2 guild can: build additional tools around the game’s ecosystem that plug directly into the game and its official tools. And as you know, development takes time, so starting early is simply smart

Thanks mate!

I try to be as complete as I can,  but I can absolutely sometimes miss a nuance or detail 

That said, let me go over your list:
The zATLAS on the PTR C4 was an audience suggestion, it's not confirmed. It was an idea (unless the SA Team confirmed it later).
Yep! Perhaps not really confirmed, but mentioned by Jose the day after during the LoreKeepers
In the BREW, I liked Jim's explanations of why PTR and why C4 took longer (it's missing in your article).
It’s literally mentioned at the top 
“To kick things off, he went into why it took so long to deliver SAGE C4:”

Regarding the “Why PTR”, the PTR is not news. The reason why we do this has been explained a long time ago, when the PTR was announced 
Key Points by JIM: “fun drives retention → retention drives economy,” plus the “lower barrier to entry on z.ink makes fun+accessibility possible,”  makes it very persuasive because he explained it using poker analogy, retention metrics, player psychology.  (I didn't see enough of it in the article).
I too like that point  In fact, I liked a ton of what Jim was saying. I listened to the recording 3 times because he said great things 
But this is not news.. For this kind of stuff people need to attend the Brew, or listen to the recording.
One caution by Jim was that automation "might" not be in PTR C4.
I am literally saying that it will come later: “Currently being implemented into Holosim, the team plans to (at a later point in time) to bring this to SAGE as well.”

I’m nowhere suggesting this could come to the PTR (though it could )

author: ! ᚺEIM | VɪᴋɪɴɢᴇɴBᴇɴɴʏViking
content: With all due respect, I find it baffling when anyone says there's no market for a product that they are using.  The very fact that there is a userbase proves that there is a market.  And that includes: the racing, FPS and Holosim which a there's a subset of the SA community that are obsessed with.  On planet Earth, there's undoubtably 100X-1000X more people that would love these games and become obsessed.  And C4 will be another game mode that will really appeal to grognards.  The best analogy comparing, C4 vs. Stellaris is: poker vs. rummy.  The fact we are playing for real money with real consequences changes everything.  Will that appeal to everyone?  No.  But there's no shortage of people that love higher risks games as proven by poker's popularity or even prediction markets.  Now, I agree that:   4X web3 games is a small niche at the moment,That game modes like racing and FPS aren't polished enough to blow away the masses yet,C4's complexity will be too much for many (but will be like crack to people who love complexity like myself)., And here's the most important question IMO:  how do we profitably market to the grognards?  It's a question I think about it almost every day.  I am working on some new PIPs that might able to have an impact.

author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content:
I'd really like to give my take here but I'm afraid it would be long and boring.
I'll just TLDR: imho the medium needed to get to the masses should not be the PC but the smartphone. Even Sony is developing games for mobile first (look at new Horizon mmo). I would never play a mobile game but apparently thats the way to go ( $100+ billions worth in 2024/25).

C4 is way too complicated for people who is starting the game but its fine not knowing ALL the game, just teach people that is completely fine learning  in time with a lot of tutorials and we are golden. The game feels the opposite of "easy to learn, hard to master" because there's A LOT of stuff to learn, not only the mechanics. We just need to tell people that is fine playing while learning.

Off topic: apparently there's been a +25% on daily transaction in SAGE in last 30 days and +5% in daily users (4 days average). Its not much but its still a positive change, Zink campaign maybe is kicking in!

content:

"Key points::
Only three companies produce advanced memory at scale: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.
These firms have massively redirected production capacity toward HBM for AI (e.g., Nvidia GPUs, hyperscaler servers), as it offers 3–5× higher margins than consumer-grade DRAM.
AI/data centers are projected to consume ~20% (or up to 70% in some reports) of global DRAM production in 2026, creating a zero-sum situation where consumer supply is starved.
Impacts include:Consumer RAM prices surging dramatically (e.g., +246% in recent months per the thread; other sources cite 50–170% jumps in 2025 with more expected in 2026).
Nvidia cutting RTX 50-series GPU production by 30–40% due to GDDR7/HBM shortages.
PC makers (Dell, Lenovo, HP) raising prices 15–30%.
Micron largely exiting consumer memory to focus on AI clients; vendors sold out through 2026–2028.
Broader ripple effects on smartphones, Intel chip production, and even auto sectors.

New memory fabs take 3–5+ years to come online → shortages likely persist into 2027–2028."

author: ! SH | Bohemian ⪛⦿⫺
content: Several aspects of this:  Chain performance + lower fee structure: not necessarily the most compelling value proposition because (in theory) you have a better opportunity for user acquisition on an already popular chain like Solana. Also, we know the fee structure is dependent on FDV., Portability: fully compatible with Solana (minimal/zero changes to consensus or agave client). This makes it easy for teams to deploy on z.ink if they've built anything for Solana. Launching on z.ink doesn't mean migrating -- can just be an expansion opportunity with minimal lift., zProfile: our most unique selling point. Introduces sybil resistance and reputation. Allows us to "pre-qualify" users for various marketing activity, making z.ink an L1, digital identity service, and a marketing platform, with the opportunity for teams launching on z.ink to become a part of various airdrop distributions and multi-pass campaigns. All while mitigating exposure to pure extractors., Grants: large allocation of tokens to these airdrops and ecosystem growth, and we can incentivize early adoption., Exposure to Star Atlas partnership: this shouldn't be underestimated. We get outreach from teams all the time wanting to partner with Star Atlas. We can leverage that interest in driving people to build on z.ink.,

author: ! SH | Bohemian ⪛⦿⫺
content: We're still refining some of the parameters around transaction fees, but very likely to remain consistent with Solana's structure. i.e. 5000 lamports (0.000005 ZINK) for a standard transaction. Fees can be updated via consensus -- so it requires support from validators. Now, this will be relatively easy with a small validator set at the start, but would need to go through some formal form of governance (ZINK is not a governance token) to update in the future. Some form of majority or super-majority to approve changes. Otherwise, we'll inherit all of the functionality that exists on Solana. So priority fees instituted should we encounter significant congestion on the network.  All fees will be paid in the ZINK token, like any other layer-1 token. There is nothing we can do reduce volatility of the token.  Yes, I'm referring to the dollar-equivalent value of fees. Given we're likely to approach tx fees in a model very similar to Solana, all things being equal, the dollar value of Solana fees is likely to be considerably higher given its market cap. Otherwise, we are in an advantageous position with z.ink because of our's and the DAO's substantial stake in the network token, earning both tx fee share and network inflation, which could conceptually be applied to some type of subsidy specifically for Star Atlas users. In theory, fee subsidies could be extended to other projects, but less likely.

author: [AEP] Funcracker [AEP]
content: It's fundamentally different from selling to Paradox. By the way, this idea isn't mine, it was actually brought up by the team during an econ forum.  The main reasoning is/was Sage isn't bringing new people in, isn't acting as a good second part of the funnel, is draining valuable DEV time, is draining SOL from the ecosystem, isn't driving primary sales up, and quite literally reached its end as far content available.  We can definitely disagree on this, that wouldn't be the first time we do. But I wouldn't call Sage ATMTA's main product anymore. It was a stepping stone, and I'm not alone in saying that it accomplished what it was designed for.  (I'm still in there, it's my main source of zXP, btw. Just... Times are tough, and shutting it down makes sense from a lot of perspectives. But also doesn't for some others. No easy path out of the current swamp we're in...).

author: [SAI] Sim [STAR]
content:
In my opinion, we are now too close to C4 for any alternative solution to “holding out” to make sense. We don’t have dates, but I don’t see C4 being possible beyond the end of March/April. If it were already clear now that this deadline cannot be met, I think it would be better to release C4 now on Solana and then migrate to Zink afterward.

I understand it was designed to handle a number of transactions an order of magnitude higher than Labs, and I know that performance—especially for combat—is critical, but at least we could start building on claim stakes and capturing neutral sectors. It would be a jolt to the stagnation that’s in the air.

I have no idea how complex what I’m proposing actually is; I’m just clinging to a message from Michael a few days ago.

Even something as simple as “copying the current state of Sage,” replicating it on Holosim C4, and playing there would be fine.

From what I understand, it would be almost like playing a Web2 game because everything would be in ATMTA’s hands, but if you think about it, in the unfortunate and unthinkable worst-case scenario, what’s the point of having assets if the game is no longer being developed?

All of this to say that, personally, I’m open to ANY solution (preferably temporary) to speed things up and simplify the process.

author: Lysimach | Make Polis Great [STAR]
content: It's fundamentally different from selling to Paradox. By the way, this idea isn't mine, it was actually brought up by the team during an econ forum.  The main reasoning is/was Sage isn't bringing new people in, isn't acting as a good second part of the funnel, is draining valuable DEV time, is draining SOL from the ecosystem, isn't driving primary sales up, and quite literally reached its end as far content available.  We can definitely disagree on this, that wouldn't be the first time we do. But I wouldn't call Sage ATMTA's main product anymore. It was a stepping stone, and I'm not alone in saying that it accomplished what it was designed for.  (I'm still in there, it's my main source of zXP, btw. Just... Times are tough, and shutting it down makes sense from a lot of perspectives. But also doesn't for some others. No easy path out of the current swamp we're in...).
